title: Glossary
markdown:
Every term from the course, in alphabetical order. The lesson that introduces each one is in brackets.

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **&str** | A borrowed string slice; string literals are `&'static str`. (2.03) |
| **Adapter** | An iterator method that wraps another iterator, such as `map`, `filter` or `zip`; nothing runs until a consumer pulls values. (5.02) |
| **Arc** | `Arc<T>`, an atomically reference-counted pointer that can be shared between threads. (6.02) |
| **AsRef** | A trait for types that can cheaply give a reference to another type. (7.02) |
| **Associated function** | A function in an `impl` block without `self`, called as `Type::name()`, such as `String::new`. (2.04) |
| **Associated type** | A type a trait leaves to each implementation, such as `Iterator::Item`. (5.03) |
| **async / await** | `async fn` returns a future instead of running; `.await` waits for a future inside another async function. (6.03) |
| **Atomic** | A type such as `AtomicU64` whose operations other threads see whole, without a lock. (6.02) |
| **Binary crate** | A crate with a `main` function that builds into a program. (3.05) |
| **Borrow** | Using a value through a reference without taking ownership. (2.02) |
| **Borrow checker** | The part of the compiler that checks every reference is valid and that `&mut` borrows are exclusive. (2.02) |
| **Box** | `Box<T>`, an owned value on the heap; used for recursive types and trait objects. (5.04) |
| **BufReader** | Wraps a reader to read in large blocks, giving line-by-line reading. (7.04) |
| **Cargo** | Rust's build tool and package manager: `cargo new`, `build`, `run`, `test`. (1.01) |
| **Channel** | A queue between threads: `mpsc::channel()` gives a sender and a receiver. (6.01) |
| **Clippy** | Cargo's linter, `cargo clippy`, which suggests clearer or faster code. (6.04) |
| **Clone** | The trait for making an explicit deep copy with `.clone()`. (2.01) |
| **Closure** | An anonymous function that can capture variables from where it is written: `\|x\| x + 1`. (5.01) |
| **Command** | `std::process::Command`: starts another program with arguments and collects its output. (7.04) |
| **Consumer** | An iterator method that pulls the values out, such as `collect`, `sum`, `count` or `for`. (5.02) |
| **Copy** | The trait for small types copied bit for bit on assignment instead of moved, such as `i32` and `bool`. (2.01) |
| **Cow** | Clone on write: holds either borrowed or owned data, allocating only when needed. (7.02) |
| **Crate** | A compilation unit: a library or a binary. Crates from crates.io are dependencies. (3.05) |
| **CStr** | A borrowed zero-terminated C string; `CString` is the owned form. (7.03) |
| **Data race** | Two threads touching the same memory at once with at least one writing; safe Rust rules them out. (6.02) |
| **Declarative macro** | A macro written with `macro_rules!`: rules that match input and produce code. (7.01) |
| **Deref coercion** | The automatic conversion of `&String` to `&str`, `&Vec<T>` to `&[T]` and `&Box<T>` to `&T`. (3.02) |
| **Derive** | `#[derive(Debug, Clone, PartialEq)]`: asking the compiler to write standard trait impls. (4.03) |
| **Doc comment** | A `///` comment that becomes documentation; its code examples run as doc tests. (6.04) |
| **Drop** | The trait whose `drop` runs when a value goes out of scope; it frees what the value owns. (2.01) |
| **dyn Trait** | A trait object: a value of some type implementing the trait, chosen at run time. (4.05) |
| **Edition** | A set of language rules (2018, 2021, 2024) chosen per crate in `Cargo.toml`. (1.01) |
| **Enum** | A type whose value is one of several variants, each of which may carry data. (2.05) |
| **ErrorKind** | The category of an `io::Error`, such as `NotFound` or `PermissionDenied`. (7.04) |
| **ExitCode** | The status a program returns from `main`; `ExitCode::SUCCESS` is 0. (7.04) |
| **Expression** | Code that produces a value; blocks, `if` and `match` are expressions in Rust. (1.03) |
| **extern "C"** | Declares functions that use the C calling convention. (7.03) |
| **FFI** | Foreign function interface: calling code written in other languages, usually C. (7.03) |
| **FnOnce, FnMut, Fn** | The closure traits: callable once (may consume captures), callable many times with changes, or without changes. (5.01) |
| **Fragment specifier** | The kind of input a macro variable matches, such as `expr`, `ident`, `ty` or `tt`. (7.01) |
| **Future** | A value that will produce a result later; it does nothing until polled by a runtime. (6.03) |
| **Generic** | Code written once for many types, with type parameters such as `T`. (4.01) |
| **HashMap** | A key-value map with fast lookup and no order. (3.03) |
| **Immutable** | Unchangeable; every variable is immutable unless declared `mut`. (1.02) |
| **impl Trait** | "Some type that implements this trait", in argument or return position. (4.02) |
| **Interior mutability** | Changing data behind a shared reference, checked at run time, as `RefCell` and `Mutex` do. (5.04) |
| **Iterator** | A trait with one required method, `next`, which returns `Option<Item>`. (5.03) |
| **Lifetime** | The span of code a reference is valid for, written `'a` when it must be named. (4.04) |
| **Lifetime elision** | The rules that let most functions leave lifetimes unwritten. (4.04) |
| **Macro** | Code that writes code, called with `!`: `println!`, `vec!`, `format!`. (1.01) |
| **Macro hygiene** | Names created inside a macro do not clash with the caller's names. (7.01) |
| **Marker trait** | A trait with no methods, used to label types for generic code. (7.05) |
| **match** | Comparing a value against patterns; the compiler checks every case is covered. (2.05) |
| **Module** | A namespace inside a crate, declared with `mod`; items are private unless `pub`. (3.05) |
| **Monomorphisation** | Compiling a separate copy of generic code for each concrete type used, so generics cost nothing at run time. (4.01) |
| **Move** | Transferring ownership; the old variable can no longer be used. (2.01) |
| **Mutex** | A lock that lets one thread at a time reach the data inside: `lock()` returns a guard. (6.02) |
| **Newtype** | A struct wrapping a single value to give it a distinct type and its own rules. (7.02) |
| **Option** | `Some(value)` or `None`: Rust's replacement for null. (2.05) |
| **Orphan rule** | You may implement a trait for a type only if your crate owns the trait or the type. (4.02) |
| **Ownership** | Every value has one owner; when the owner goes out of scope, the value is dropped. (2.01) |
| **Panic** | Stopping the thread because of a bug, such as an out-of-range index or `unwrap` on `None`. (3.04) |
| **Path** | A borrowed file system path; `PathBuf` is the owned form. (7.04) |
| **Pattern** | A shape to match against: literals, ranges, `\|`, bindings, `@`, struct and tuple patterns, guards. (5.05) |
| **PhantomData** | A zero-size field that marks a type parameter as used without storing it. (7.05) |
| **Pin** | `Pin<&mut T>`, a pointer that promises the value will not move; futures are polled through it. (6.03) |
| **Prelude** | The names every Rust file imports automatically, such as `Vec`, `Option` and `String`. (1.05) |
| **Procedural macro** | A Rust function that receives code as tokens and returns new code, used for `derive`. (7.01) |
| **Raw pointer** | `*const T` or `*mut T`: a pointer with no lifetime or validity guarantee. (7.03) |
| **Rc** | `Rc<T>`, a reference-counted pointer for shared ownership within one thread. (5.04) |
| **RefCell** | A cell that checks borrowing rules at run time, allowing changes through `&`. (5.04) |
| **Reference** | `&T` (shared, read-only) or `&mut T` (exclusive, may change): a pointer that borrows. (2.02) |
| **Result** | `Ok(value)` or `Err(error)`: how Rust functions report recoverable failure. (3.04) |
| **Safety contract** | The conditions a caller must uphold for an `unsafe fn`, written in its `# Safety` section. (7.03) |
| **Scoped thread** | A thread started with `thread::scope` that may borrow local data, because it is joined before the scope ends. (6.01) |
| **Sealed trait** | A trait that code outside the crate cannot implement, thanks to a private supertrait. (7.05) |
| **Send** | The marker trait for types that may move to another thread. (6.02) |
| **Shadowing** | Declaring a new variable with an existing name, often to change its type. (1.02) |
| **Slice** | A view into part of a sequence: `&[T]` or `&str`. (2.03) |
| **Smart pointer** | A type that acts like a pointer and owns or manages its target: `Box`, `Rc`, `Arc`. (5.04) |
| **Statement** | Code that does something but produces no value; a trailing `;` turns an expression into one. (1.03) |
| **String** | An owned, growable UTF-8 text buffer. (1.05) |
| **Struct** | A type that groups named fields. (2.04) |
| **Sync** | The marker trait for types that many threads may use through shared references at once. (6.02) |
| **The ? operator** | Returns early with the error from a `Result` (or `None` from an `Option`), converting the error with `From`. (3.04) |
| **Trait** | A set of methods a type can implement; Rust's interfaces. (4.02) |
| **Trait bound** | A requirement on a type parameter, such as `T: Display + Clone`. (4.01) |
| **Trait object** | A `dyn Trait` value behind a pointer, called through a vtable. (4.05) |
| **Turbofish** | `::<T>`, naming a generic type at the call: `"5".parse::<i32>()`. (4.01) |
| **Type-state** | Representing each state of an object as a different type, so wrong orders do not compile. (7.05) |
| **Unit type** | `()`, the type of "no meaningful value". (1.03) |
| **unsafe** | A block or function where five extra operations are allowed and the programmer guarantees safety. (7.03) |
| **unwrap** | Taking the value out of an `Option` or `Result`, panicking if there is none. (3.04) |
| **UTF-8** | The encoding of Rust strings: a character takes 1 to 4 bytes, so strings are not indexed by number. (3.02) |
| **Vec** | `Vec<T>`, a growable array on the heap. (3.01) |
| **Workspace** | Several crates built together with one `Cargo.lock`. (6.04) |
